adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The computed schema keys z.string().toString() and z.string().optional().toString() evaluate to the literal string "[object Object]", so the second (optional) key silently overwrites the first and minimumTokenResponseSchema is effectively {access_token: string} — it neither validates the intended numeric expiry field nor retains any extra field. In sync mode every refreshed token response is stripped down to access_token alone: expiry data from the sync endpoint is discarded (callers fall back to stale expiry, causing repeated spurious refreshes), and any contract the sync endpoint was supposed to honor is not actually enforced.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`, `minimumTokenResponseSchema` uses computed keys like `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]`. These are evaluated immediately to literal property names (whatever `toString()` returns for those Zod schema objects), not a wildcard/index signature. As a result, the schema does not actually validate “any numeric expiry field” nor “allow other properties”; it will only accept token responses that contain those specific literal keys, and otherwise `safeParse` will fail and `parseRefreshTokenResponse` will throw `Invalid refreshed tokens were returned` in sync mode. The finding’s exact claim about both keys becoming `"[object Object]"` and overwriting down to `{access_token}` isn’t guaranteed from the diff, but the underlying issue (schema is broken and doesn’t enforce the intended contract) is a real defect introduced here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The refresh_token placeholder injection (data.refresh_token = "refresh_token") runs unconditionally — including in the non-sync path where the caller passes the real provider schema — and office365calendar's refreshAccessToken spreads tokenResponse.data over the existing credentials, so a response lacking refresh_token overwrites the stored real refresh token with the literal string "refresh_token". For a deployment without credential sync, one refresh cycle in which Microsoft omits refresh_token permanently replaces the user's real refresh token with a placeholder in the database; all subsequent refreshes fail and the user must reinstall the app.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`, after a successful `safeParse` it unconditionally injects a placeholder when `refresh_token` is missing: `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token";` (this runs for both the sync and non-sync branches). In `packages/app-store/office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts`, the refreshed token payload (`tokenResponse.data`) is spread over the existing credentials (`o365AuthCredentials = { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...(tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data) };`) and then persisted to DB. If the parsed token response lacks `refresh_token` but still passes the schema, the injected literal string will overwrite the real stored refresh token, causing permanent breakage until reinstall.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The iteration silently changed failure semantics for the pre-existing path: the console.error zodError logging was removed and the code now throws via parseRefreshTokenResponse on schema failure, ungated by APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED. Existing self-hosters who never enable credential sync lose the previous graceful behavior (log and continue with stale-but-usable credentials) and instead get a thrown error on any malformed Microsoft token response — an objective change smuggled into the sync PR without being called out for acceptance.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts`, the prior code used `refreshTokenResponseSchema.safeParse(responseJson)` and, on failure, only `console.error(...)` while continuing with the existing `o365AuthCredentials` (i.e., effectively keeping stale credentials) and proceeding to `prisma.credential.update(...)`. The new code replaces this with `parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseJson, refreshTokenResponseSchema)`, which (per `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`) throws `new Error("Invalid refreshed tokens were returned")` on any schema failure regardless of `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` (the flag only changes which schema is used, not whether it throws). This is a verifiable change to failure semantics for non-sync deployments and can turn previously non-fatal malformed/changed Microsoft token responses into hard failures.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] This block adds an unconditional Salesforce token refresh (remote POST + credential DB write) on the connection-creation path that previously served directly from cached credentialKey, plus a hardcoded login.salesforce.com URL and a dead `if (!accessTokenParsed.success)` check (parseRefreshTokenResponse already throws on failure). Every Salesforce calendar operation pays an extra token-endpoint round-trip and a DB write per connection creation, a hot-path regression unrelated to the stated credential-sync objective that entered the PR without its own acceptance; the hardcoded URL also ignores instance_url for custom Salesforce domains.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows SalesforceCalendarService now unconditionally performs a refresh-token POST to `https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token` and then immediately persists the result via `prisma.credential.update(...)` before returning a `new jsforce.Connection(...)` (see added block in `packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts`). This means connection creation now always incurs a network round-trip and DB write, which is a concrete hot-path/performance/architecture concern (even if it may still work correctly). adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The webhook secret is compared with a plain !== string comparison rather than a timing-safe comparison. A self-hoster enabling credential sync exposes CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET to a remote timing side channel over this unauthenticated endpoint; an attacker who recovers it can push arbitrary credentials into any user's account.

adjudication.rationale: New webhook endpoint `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts` authenticates solely by comparing a request header to `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` using `!==` (strict string compare). This is not timing-safe and can leak information about the secret via timing differences during comparison, and if the secret is recovered the handler allows creating/updating credentials for arbitrary `userId`/`appSlug` (`prisma.credential.update/create`).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The decrypted keys are JSON.parse'd and stored directly as credential.key with no validation against the app's credential schema, and JSON.parse/symmetricDecrypt failures propagate as unhandled 500s. A malformed or wrong-shape payload from the parent instance poisons the user's credential silently (the webhook returns 200), and the integration then fails at usage time with schema/crash errors that are far from the actual cause; any thrown ZodError/JSON parse error also surfaces as a 500 instead of the 4xx the contract implies.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added webhook handler (`apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`), the decrypted payload is handled as `const keys = JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` and then written directly to `prisma.credential.update/create` as `key: keys` with no validation against any app-specific credential schema. Additionally, there is no try/catch around `symmetricDecrypt` or `JSON.parse`, so a bad secret, bad ciphertext, or invalid JSON will throw and result in an unhandled 500 rather than a controlled 4xx response. For any wrong-shape but JSON-valid payload, the endpoint still returns 200 after persisting it, potentially poisoning stored credentials.

Callers sending a bad payload (or an attacker probing the endpoint) receive a 500 server error, polluting error monitoring and misrepresenting client-side input errors as server faults.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The findFirst-then-update/create sequence is not atomic, and the inline comment acknowledges upsert was rejected — two concurrent webhooks for the same userId+appId both observe no credential and both create one. Concurrent credential-sync deliveries for the same user produce duplicate Credential rows for the same app, after which findFirst picks an arbitrary one for updates and the stale duplicate keeps being used or refreshed inconsistently.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added webhook handler `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the code does `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId }})` and then conditionally `update` or `create`. That read-then-write sequence is not atomic; two concurrent requests for the same `(userId, appId)` can both observe “no credential” and proceed to `credential.create(...)`. The diff does not show any DB-level unique constraint on `(userId, appId)` that would prevent duplicates, and the inline comment explicitly notes avoiding `upsert`, reinforcing the finding’s core concurrency concern.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is declared as a constant but its value is the string|undefined result of an && of two env vars (not a boolean), and the enablement condition `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` is hand-duplicated in parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts and refreshOAuthTokens.ts. TypeScript will not flag boolean misuse of the constant, and the next change to the gating (e.g., adding a third env var) applied to only one of the two duplicated sites leaves token fetching and token parsing half-enabled, producing refreshes from the sync endpoint parsed with the wrong schema.

However, as written, the truthiness checks will behave correctly, so this is not a current verifiable functional defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The webhook secret is verified with a plain `!==` string comparison (`req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`), which is not constant-time, and the endpoint has no rate limiting on the secret check. An attacker who can reach this endpoint can mount a timing side-channel (assisted by unthrottled retry) against the shared secret; each recovered secret grants the ability to inject/overwrite OAuth credentials for ANY userId, i.e. takeover of arbitrary users' calendar/CRM integrations. The correct control is a constant-time comparison (e.g. crypto.timingSafeEqual) plus rate limiting, neither of which exists in this diff.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added webhook handler `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the shared secret is checked via a normal equality comparison: `req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME || "calcom-webhook-secret"] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. This is not a constant-time comparison, and the handler shows no throttling/rate-limiting around the secret check, so repeated attempts are unmitigated. Additionally, the endpoint allows creating/updating a credential for an arbitrary `userId` once the secret check passes (it only verifies the user/app exist), so authentication strength of this secret check is security-critical. (The finding’s claim that recovering only the webhook secret is sufficient for full credential injection is somewhat overstated because the payload is also decrypted with `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, which is not provided to the attacker in the diff.)

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Authentication for a credential-injection endpoint that can write keys for any userId rests on a single static, non-rotatable shared header value, with no HMAC signature, timestamp, or nonce, so valid requests are replayable by design and one leaked secret compromises every user at once. Whoever captures one legitimate webhook request (proxy logs, the plaintext custom header on a non-TLS self-hosted deployment) can replay it indefinitely, and any operator of any child instance holding the shared secret can write credentials into any other instance/user reachable with the same secret. There is no per-request binding, no replay window, and no way to rotate without coordinating every deployment.

adjudication.rationale: The newly added webhook endpoint `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts` authorizes requests solely by checking a single shared header value against `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` (`req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME||"calcom-webhook-secret"] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`). The request body includes an arbitrary `userId` and `appSlug`, and on success the handler updates/creates `prisma.credential` for that `userId` with decrypted `keys`, with no per-request signature/HMAC, timestamp, nonce, or replay window. This makes captured valid requests replayable and makes the shared secret a single point of compromise for writing credentials for any userId, which is a concrete security defect shown by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The decrypted credential payload is `JSON.parse`d and written directly to `credential.key` with no schema validation at this trust boundary. Anything the sender produces (a misconfigured encryption key, a buggy sync sender, or a holder of the webhook secret) is persisted verbatim as the app's credential; the malformed shape surfaces only later, inside booking/calendar flows that consume `credential.key`, causing hard-to-trace runtime failures far from the write that caused them.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added webhook endpoint `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the decrypted credential payload is `JSON.parse(...)`d from `symmetricDecrypt(...)` and then persisted directly into Prisma `credential.key` via `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key: keys } })` / `create({ data: { key: keys, ... } })` with no schema validation of `keys`. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is implicitly truthy whenever both `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` and `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` are set, with no explicit opt-in flag. An operator who sets CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET for any other webhook purpose silently activates the new public credential-injection endpoint and switches all OAuth token refreshes to the sync endpoint — a security-posture and behavior change triggered by environment presence rather than a deliberate feature flag that can be turned off without a code change.

adjudication.rationale: The diff defines `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` as the truthiness of two env vars (`process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY`, in `packages/lib/constants.ts`). The new public API route `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts` gates access only on that boolean (plus header secret match), so merely setting those env vars enables the credential-injection endpoint without any explicit opt-in flag. This is a real behavior/security posture change triggered by env presence rather than a deliberate feature toggle. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] When sharing is enabled, `minimumTokenResponseSchema` strips every field except `access_token` (the computed `[z.string().toString()]` keys collapse to a single literal non-matching key), so `data.refresh_token` is always undefined and the code overwrites the credential's real refresh token with the literal string `"refresh_token"`, which callers then persist via `prisma.credential.update`. The first token refresh under sharing mode irreversibly replaces stored refresh tokens with the placeholder for providers whose refresh path goes through parse (office365, zoom, webex, lark, zoho). If the sync endpoint is ever unreachable, the feature is disabled, or the deployment falls back to direct refresh, every affected credential is dead and users must re-authenticate — a destructive, one-way write performed automatically on the normal refresh path.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `parseRefreshTokenResponse` with a `minimumTokenResponseSchema` that uses computed keys like `[z.string().toString()]`, which in JS/Zod collapses to a single literal property key rather than “any string key”. This means the schema will not properly retain/accept provider fields (including `refresh_token`), and because Zod objects strip unknown keys by default, `refresh_token` will be absent from `refreshTokenResponse.data`. The function then unconditionally fills it with the literal string `"refresh_token"` when missing. Call sites such as `Office365CalendarService` spread `tokenResponse.data` back into the stored credential and persist via `prisma.credential.update`, so the refresh token can be clobbered under sharing mode. Regardless, the `minimumTokenResponseSchema` as written is itself invalid for the intended purpose and will likely break refresh parsing under sharing mode.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] A token refresh fetch to login.salesforce.com plus a `prisma.credential.update` now runs unconditionally on every SalesforceCalendarService construction, with no expiry check, where previously the service constructed its connection without any remote call. Every calendar operation touching Salesforce (availability checks, booking flows) pays a synchronous remote token-refresh round trip and a credential DB write, multiplying load on the Salesforce token endpoint and risking throttling/bans that turn into booking-path failures; the guarded refresh the expiry timestamp exists for was replaced by an unconditional one.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts`, a refresh-token request to `https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token` is now executed before creating the `jsforce.Connection`, followed by `await prisma.credential.update(...)`, with no conditional guard/expiry check shown in the diff. This means constructing/initializing the service will always incur a remote round-trip plus a DB write, which is a concrete perf/operational concern (rate limiting/throttling risk) grounded in the added code, even if it may not be a strict functional correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The credential-sync webhook persists the result of JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...)) into Credential.key with no schema validation, and the update branch (prisma.credential.update with data: { key: keys }) wholesale replaces the existing credential key, so any in-range-but-malformed sync payload permanently overwrites a previously valid credential with no backup or recovery step. A parent application that sends a wrong-shaped or truncated keys blob (or a key encrypted with a mismatched CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY that still decrypts to parseable JSON) silently destroys the user's working integration credentials on the next sync; every subsequent calendar/video call for that user fails until manual re-auth, and the prior key values are unrecoverable because no audit/backfill of the overwritten data exists. Every other credential write in this diff validates via a zod schema (googleCredentialSchema, zoomRefreshedTokenSchema, salesforceTokenSchema) before persisting; this write path alone bypasses that, and unlike the read-side parseRefreshTokenResponse calls it has no schema at all.

adjudication.rationale: In the new webhook handler `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the decrypted payload is persisted directly: `const keys = JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` and then `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key: keys } })` (or `create` with `key: keys`) with no app-specific schema validation or shape checking before overwriting the existing `Credential.key`. This means any JSON-decryptable but wrong/malformed payload can permanently replace a previously valid credential record, causing downstream integration failures with no recovery path shown in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the safeParse wrapper object ({success, data, error}), but Google CalendarService assigns it directly as the credential key (previously googleCredentialSchema.parse returned the unwrapped data), so the first token refresh persists {success: true, data: {...}} as credential.key. After the first refresh in shared-credential mode, every subsequent read of credential.key in the Google Calendar service sees the wrapper shape instead of the token object; access_token/refresh_token/expiry_date lookups resolve to undefined, silently breaking all Google Calendar sync for that user (bookings fail or silently skip calendar writes). Note Salesforce's call site correctly consumes .data, confirming the function's return shape and that the Google call site is wrong.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`, the function returns the Zod `safeParse` result object (`{ success, data, error }`), not the parsed `data`. In `packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts`, the refreshed credential is persisted as `key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema)` and then written to Prisma (`data: { key }`), which would store the wrapper shape in `credential.key` instead of the token payload. Other call sites (e.g., Office365 and Salesforce) treat the return value as a wrapper and access `.data`, confirming the intended return shape and that Google’s call site is incorrect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] When credential sharing is enabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns a raw fetch Response object, but googlecalendar expects {res: {data}} (reads res?.data then token.access_token), hubspot expects a HubspotToken, and zoho/zoho-bigin expect an axios response (read tokenInfo.data.error), so the sync path structurally cannot satisfy any of these callers. With APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED on, every token refresh on the Google path throws TypeError reading .access_token of undefined, Hubspot reads accessToken off a Response (undefined), and zoho-bigin/zohocrm throw TypeError on tokenInfo.data.error — every shared-mode calendar refresh crashes instead of returning a token, so booking flows that depend on these integrations fail. Additionally the sync endpoint's response.ok is never checked, so a 401/500 from the sync service is handed to callers as if it were a token response.

adjudication.rationale: In shared mode (`APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT && userId`), `refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw `fetch(...)` Response (`packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts`) instead of the shape expected by multiple callers. For example, Google Calendar assigns `const res = await refreshOAuthTokens(...)` and then does `const token = res?.data; googleCredentials.access_token = token.access_token` (`packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts`), but a `Response` has no `.data`, so `token` becomes `undefined` and `token.access_token` will throw. Zoho Bigin/Zoho CRM expect an axios response and access `tokenInfo.data...` (`packages/app-store/zoho-bigin/lib/CalendarService.ts`, `packages/app-store/zohocrm/lib/CalendarService.ts`), which will also throw with a `Response`. Hubspot similarly expects a `HubspotToken` object but may receive a `Response` (`packages/app-store/hubspot/lib/CalendarService.ts`). Additionally, the shared-mode path never checks `response.ok`, so non-2xx responses are passed through as if valid token refresh results.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body) is uncaught, so any malformed body (including a GET or empty POST to this route) throws a ZodError that Next converts to a raw 500 instead of the 400 the request shape warrants. A sender's first debugging signal for a payload typo is a 500 with a stack trace rather than a 4xx validation error; retry logic on the Cal.com side treats 500s as transient and re-sends, amplifying bad payloads.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added API route `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the handler calls `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` without any try/catch or use of `safeParse`. If the request body is missing/malformed (e.g., empty POST or GET with no body), Zod will throw a `ZodError`, which Next.js will treat as an unhandled exception and respond with a 500. The route also does not restrict HTTP methods before parsing, making such malformed requests more likely to hit this path.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, ...)) is unguarded, so a payload encrypted with a mismatched key, truncated ciphertext, or valid ciphertext of non-JSON plaintext throws and surfaces as a 500. Key rotation or partial deployments where Cal.com and the self-hosted instance disagree on CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY turn every sync webhook into a 500 instead of a 4xx, making the real config problem look like a server crash.

adjudication.rationale: In the new API route `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the decrypted payload is immediately `JSON.parse`d with no error handling: `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY || ""))`. If `symmetricDecrypt` throws (bad/mismatched key, truncated/invalid ciphertext) or returns non-JSON plaintext, `JSON.parse` will throw and the handler has no try/catch, so the request will surface as an unhandled error/500 rather than a controlled 4xx response. This is directly verifiable from the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Both computed keys in minimumTokenResponseSchema evaluate to the identical string (both derive from z.string().toString()), so the z.number() catchall on line 8 is overwritten by the z.unknown().optional() key on line 9, and zod's default key stripping then removes every field except access_token from the parsed data. In shared-credential mode the 'expiry' property the schema claims to capture (expiry_date, expires_in) is silently dropped from refreshed tokens; callers that persist .data store a credential with no expiry, so expiry-based freshness checks treat the token as always expired and re-hit the sync endpoint on every calendar operation.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`, `minimumTokenResponseSchema` is defined as `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), [z.string().toString()]: z.number(), [z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional() })`. Those computed property keys are evaluated immediately as JavaScript strings and will collide (both derive from calling `.toString()` on a Zod schema object), so one overwrites the other in the object literal. Additionally, `z.object(...)` does not implement a wildcard/index-signature this way; unknown keys are stripped by default, so fields like `expiry_date`/`expires_in` will not be retained under this schema. Since `parseRefreshTokenResponse` uses this minimum schema in shared-credential mode, it can indeed drop expiry fields from the parsed data, impacting refresh logic/persistence.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] When the sync-endpoint response lacks refresh_token, the code writes the literal placeholder string "refresh_token" into the parsed data, which callers like office365calendar spread over the stored credential key (o365AuthCredentials = {...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data}), overwriting the real refresh token. The user's real OAuth refresh token is silently destroyed and replaced with a constant; if APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED or CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT is later unset, the credential can never be refreshed again and the integration dies with an opaque provider error.

adjudication.rationale: The new helper `parseRefreshTokenResponse` explicitly injects a placeholder refresh token when the parsed response lacks one: `if (!refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token) { refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"; }` (packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts). In Office365 token refresh, the returned `.data` is spread into the existing credential object: `o365AuthCredentials = { ...o365AuthCredentials, ...(tokenResponse.success && tokenResponse.data) };` (packages/app-store/office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts). If the sync endpoint / minimum schema path returns no `refresh_token`, this spread will overwrite the real stored `refresh_token` with the constant string, causing silent credential corruption and future refresh failures.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The fetch to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT has no timeout/AbortSignal, making it a timeout-less outbound call on the token-refresh path which executes inside user-facing booking and calendar operations. A hung or slow sync endpoint stalls each affected calendar operation for the platform's default connect/idle timeouts (undici: minutes), piling up concurrent booking requests and worker capacity on a dependency that is not on any critical provider's SLA.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts`, the code calls `fetch(process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, { method: "POST", body: new URLSearchParams(...) })` with no `AbortSignal`/timeout handling. This new network dependency is then used on token refresh paths (e.g., Google/Office365/Zoom/Webex/etc. services now call `refreshOAuthTokens(...)`), so a slow/hung sync endpoint can stall those operations. The diff does not implement any timeout/cancellation, so the concern is diff-grounded, but it’s primarily a resilience/availability issue rather than a deterministic functional correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The response validity check uses response.statusText !== "OK" instead of response.ok; statusText is an empty string on HTTP/2 responses and is not guaranteed across runtimes, so a successful 200 token response is rejected as an error. Salesforce calendar connections throw HttpError 400 with an empty message on refreshes that actually succeeded, breaking the integration in environments where login.salesforce.com is served over HTTP/2.
matched_golden_ids: The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate issue describes the same core bug: the integration checks `response.statusText` (e.g., comparing to "OK") rather than using `response.ok` to determine success for OAuth token refresh responses, which can misclassify successful responses and break authentication/refresh behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The zoho-bigin call site passes credentialId as the third argument of refreshOAuthTokens, whose contract (per every other call site and the sync payload field name calcomUserId) expects the Cal.com user id, so the sync endpoint is asked for credentials belonging to the wrong identity. In shared-credential mode the sync request carries the credential row id as calcomUserId, so the parent application either returns another user's credentials (which get stored under this user's credential) or fails, and the failure is surfaced only as a downstream token-parse error, not as a wrong-identifier error.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts`, the third parameter is explicitly `userId: number | null` and is sent to the sync endpoint as `calcomUserId` (via `userId.toString()`). Nearly all updated call sites pass `credential.userId`. However, in `packages/app-store/zoho-bigin/lib/CalendarService.ts`, the call is `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoho-bigin", credentialId)`, which is inconsistent and (given the name and surrounding patterns) indicates a credential-row id is being passed where a Cal.com user id is required. This would cause the sync endpoint to be queried with the wrong identity (`calcomUserId`), matching the finding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The Salesforce service constructor now unconditionally performs a remote POST to login.salesforce.com plus a prisma.credential.update on every instantiation, whereas previously the connection was built from the stored token without any eager refresh or DB write. Every calendar operation that constructs the service (listing events, booking checks) now costs a network round-trip to Salesforce and a credential write even when the stored token is still valid; a transient Salesforce outage converts every read into an exception raised from object construction.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts`, new logic performs an OAuth refresh POST to `https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token` and then `await prisma.credential.update(...)` before returning a `new jsforce.Connection(...)`, with no conditional check for token expiry/validity. This means constructing/initializing the connection path now incurs a network round-trip and DB write and will throw on non-OK responses (`if (response.statusText !== "OK") throw ...`), matching the finding’s performance/availability concern. The diff doesn’t prove it happens literally inside a synchronous `constructor`, but it is clearly on the connection-creation path and is unconditional.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The findFirst-then-create/update sequence is not atomic (the code comment rules out upsert, but no unique constraint or transaction guards userId+appId), so two concurrent webhook deliveries both observe no existing credential and both create one. Cal.com webhook retries and concurrent sync events produce duplicate credentials for the same user+app; whichever credential the app later picks may be the stale one, and the duplicate is never reconciled.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added webhook handler `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, credentials are synchronized via a non-atomic `findFirst` (by `userId` + `appId`) followed by either `credential.update` or `credential.create`. This check-then-act pattern can race under concurrent webhook deliveries: two requests can both observe no row and both execute `create`, producing duplicates unless a DB-level unique constraint exists and is handled. The diff shows no transaction/locking, no unique constraint enforcement, and no handling of a potential unique violation on `create`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The decrypted keys payload is persisted as credential.key with no validation against the target app's credential schema (e.g. googleCredentialSchema), unlike every other write path in this diff which parses before storing. A parent-application bug or schema drift silently stores a structurally invalid credential; the failure only appears later when the user's calendar/video integration throws an opaque parse or undefined-access error at use time, far from the sync event that caused it.

adjudication.rationale: In the new webhook handler (`apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`), the decrypted payload is `JSON.parse(...)`d and then persisted directly via `prisma.credential.update/create({ data: { key: keys, ... }})` with no Zod/schema validation of `keys` for the given `appSlug`/`appMetadata` (unlike other paths in this diff that parse token/credential shapes before updating the DB, e.g. `googleCredentialSchema` / `parseRefreshTokenResponse`). This is a diff-grounded data integrity/robustness concern (invalid structures can be stored and only fail later), but it’s not an immediately verifiable broken behavior since the webhook contract may intentionally allow arbitrary key shapes per app.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The removal of the refreshTokenResponseSchema.safeParse failure branch also removed the console.error that logged the zod error and the raw Microsoft response, and its replacement throws a generic 'Invalid refreshed tokens were returned'. Operators debugging Outlook refresh failures lose the only artifact that identified what Microsoft actually returned (the error shape and response body), turning a previously diagnosable failure into an unattributable one.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/office365calendar/lib/CalendarService.ts`, the previous `if (!tokenResponse.success) { console.error(..., tokenResponse.error, ..., responseJson) }` branch was removed when switching from `refreshTokenResponseSchema.safeParse(responseJson)` to `parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseJson, refreshTokenResponseSchema)`. The new helper (`packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`) throws `new Error("Invalid refreshed tokens were returned")` on parse failure and does not log the Zod error or the raw Microsoft response body. This is a real observability/debuggability regression for operators, but it doesn't by itself prove functional breakage.
